issue_context.title: Active Record class method scope leak
issue_context.body:
Active Record leaks scope on class methods directly defined on the model. This behavior is different than queries constructed within a `scope` definition. This issue is an extension of https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/32380

### Steps to reproduce
```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true

require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"

  git_source(:github) { |repo| "https://github.com/#{repo}.git" }

  gem "rails", github: "rails/rails", branch: "main"
  gem "sqlite3"
end

require "active_record"
require "minitest/autorun"
require "logger"

# This connection will do for database-independent bug reports.
ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(adapter: "sqlite3", database: ":memory:")
ActiveRecord::Base.logger = Logger.new(STDOUT)

ActiveRecord::Schema.define do
  create_table :topics, force: true do |t|
    t.references :topics, :parent
  end
end

class Topic < ActiveRecord::Base
  # NOTE: Removing the class methods below and replacing with these
  # scope calls will cause the assert to pass
  #
  # scope :toplevel, -> { where(parent_id: nil) }
  # scope :children, -> { where.not(parent_id: nil) }
  # scope :has_children, -> { where(id: Topic.children.select(:parent_id)) }

  def self.toplevel
    where(parent_id: nil)
  end

  def self.children
    where.not(parent_id: nil)
  end

  def self.has_children
    where(id: Topic.children.select(:parent_id))
  end
end

class BugTest < Minitest::Test
  def test_association_stuff
    parent_topic = Topic.create!
    Topic.create!(parent_id: parent_topic.id)

    assert_equal 1, Topic.toplevel.has_children.count
  end
end
```

### Expected behavior
Chained class methods do not leak scope

### Actual behavior
```
Failure:
BugTest#test_association_stuff [bug_report.rb:54]:
Expected: 1
Actual: 0
```

### System configuration
**Rails version**: 7.0.2.3 and main

**Ruby version**: 2.7.0
comments:
SQL when using `self.` methods (fails):

```
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM "topics" WHERE "topics"."parent_id" IS NULL AND "topics"."id" IN (SELECT "topics"."parent_id" FROM "topics" WHERE "topics"."parent_id" IS NULL AND "topics"."parent_id" IS NOT NULL)
```

SQL when using scopes (passes):

```
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM "topics" WHERE "topics"."parent_id" IS NULL AND "topics"."id" IN (SELECT "topics"."parent_id" FROM "topics" WHERE "topics"."parent_id" IS NOT NULL)
```
@kamipo it seems like the behavior should be the same in both cases, do you agree?

@ghiculescu @skipkayhil Should we keep this one open?  

(I'll stop @ notifying after this message. Just wanted to give this issue one last chance since it's still applicable as far as I'm aware)

I don't think it's possible to change this; it's a consequence of the method existing directly on the class instance.

While #32380 was able to draw this distinction for scopes, because we can control/affect the `self` that block sees, here we have a real method, which is defined where it's defined.

Notably, in scopes, `self` acts as the chained relation, while an explicit reference to `ThisModel` will start a new clean chain. It's impossible to recreate that for a class method, because `self` _is_ `ThisModel`: either both produce a chained relation (the current and established behaviour), or both start a new chain.

Beyond the compatibility concerns of making any change, having all class methods work in a cleanroom would break any method that _isn't_ a pure scope-like function:

```ruby
class ThisModel < ApplicationRecord
  def self.greet
    each { |m| puts "hello, #{m.name}" }
  end

  def self.newbies
    where(joined_at: Date.yesterday..)
  end
end

ThisModel.newbies.greet
```

I think the only reasonable option here is to note that scopes exist -- even though we also magically lift class methods onto relations -- because they are able to better support this nuance; if you need to specifically reference unscoped class from a method that may be called from a chained relation, a scope may be a better fit.

This would not be the first time that `scope` behave differently from class methods

```ruby
  scope :toplevel, -> { where(parent_id: nil) if has_hierarchy? }
  scope :children, -> { where.not(parent_id: nil) }

  def self.has_hierarchy?
    false
  end

  self.toplevel.children
```

Would work since a scope proc returning `nil` has the same meaning as `all`

But 

```ruby
  def self.toplevel
    where(parent_id: nil) if has_hierarchy?
  end

  def self.children
    where.not(parent_id: nil)
  end

  def self.has_hierarchy?
    false
  end

  self.toplevel.children
```

Would fail with `NoMethodError children on nil`.

For anyone that has a class method you can't easily convert to a scope (e.g. you need to return `nil` to the caller) append `default_scoped` to the beginning of the method chain.

Modifying the original test script like so will make the assertion pass:

```rb
def self.has_children
  where(id: Topic.default_scoped.children.select(:parent_id))
end
```

This works regardless of whether you actually have a default scope defined on the model. I believe you can essentially treat `Topic.default_scoped.where(...)` within a class method the same way you would `Topic.where(...)` called anywhere else in your application code.
